headline_en: Son went abroad by an illegal route without his father's knowledge; family speechless at his death
summary_en: Sujon Faraji of Madaripur Sadar, who left for Italy via Dubai and Libya with a broker under a BDT 15 lakh deal, is among the 23 bodies washed ashore in Libya after a boat with 56 people sank in the Mediterranean on 25 January 2025. The broker, Monir Sheikh of Rajoir, is absconding. Madaripur police have asked families of the dead and missing to file written complaints.

facts.statement: According to the Bangladesh embassy in Libya, a boat carrying 56 migrants trying to cross the Mediterranean from Libya to Italy sank on 25 January 2025; 23 bodies washed up on the beach between 28 and 31 January 2025. The decomposed bodies could not be identified, but the embassy, citing local sources, says almost all were Bangladeshi.

Sujon Faraji of Purba Ghatmajhi, Ghatmajhi union, Madaripur Sadar upazila, is among the 23 bodies washed ashore in Libya; his father Mirajul Islam confirmed the death to Prothom Alo on Tuesday 4 February 2025.

Sujon Faraji left home for Italy in late November 2024 lured by a broker: he first flew Dhaka to Dubai, stayed there a few days, then went to Libya, where he was kept in a detention house (bondishala) in Benghazi. On 24 January 2025 he and other migrants set off from the Libyan coast for Italy in an engine boat, which sank before reaching Italy.

Broker Monir Sheikh made a contract with Sujon Faraji to take him to Italy via Libya for BDT 15 lakh. Sujon's father said he learned on 25 January that Sujon had taken BDT 15 lakh from his paternal aunt and gone to Libya; an aunt provided the money.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's inquiry; father Mirajul Islam; aunt Shiuli Begum

facts.statement: The broker who took Sujon Faraji toward Italy via Libya is Monir Sheikh, son of Haidar Sheikh, of Majumdarkandi, Rajoir upazila, Madaripur. When the reporter visited, his house was locked and his mobile phone was switched off. A neighbour, Tutul Mia, said Monir has very strong 'mafia connections', has earned trust by successfully sending many young men to Italy and earned a lot of money, and is now absconding after his name came up in several recent incidents.

Madaripur Additional Superintendent of Police (Administration and Finance) Bhaskar Saha said every family of those missing or dead in Libya has been told to file a written complaint at the police station; police will then register cases and take legal action. Police have traced several accused brokers and operations to arrest them are continuing.

Sujon Faraji had finished higher secondary at a local college and drove an easybike for a few days; he chose the illegal route after not getting a chance to go to Italy legally. His father had refused to let him take the risk and was not told he had left; the family told the father he was at his aunt's house.

headline_en: Bangladesh will strengthen bilateral cooperation with Saudi Arabia on labour and migration: Adviser Asif Nazrul
summary_en: A press release on Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul's meetings in Riyadh on 30 January 2025 with Saudi HRSD and interior vice ministers and with Oman's labour deputy minister. Topics included high iqama renewal fees, workers getting contracts before departure, delays in attesting professional certificates at the Saudi embassy in Dhaka, a Saudi task force on illegal workers, repatriation of irregular migrants, a royal pardon request, and Oman's work visa suspension since 31 October 2023.

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Adviser Asif Nazrul held formal meetings in Riyadh on Thursday 30 January 2025 with Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development (HRSD) Vice Minister Abdullah Abuthnain and Interior Ministry Vice Minister Nasser bin Abdulaziz Al Dawood.
The adviser thanked Saudi Arabia for hosting more than 30 lakh (3 million) Bangladeshi workers.

Asif Nazrul invited Saudi authorities to inspect Technical Training Centres (TTCs) in Bangladesh and to consider giving skills recognition to certain centres; Saudi Arabia responded positively and agreed to a possible evaluation of TTCs.
The meeting mainly discussed the high iqama renewal fee and workers becoming jobless because of it. Saudi Arabia said its labour law is being reformed so that the rights of both sides are protected.
The two sides discussed ensuring that workers definitely receive their employment contract before leaving Bangladesh.

Bangladesh raised the problem of attestation of professional certificates at the Saudi embassy in Dhaka: the process is being delayed because there is no cultural attache. Saudi authorities assured it would be resolved quickly.
Saudi officials said a task force will soon be formed to remove the problem of illegal workers and recruitment irregularities, and welcomed Bangladesh's proposal to form a joint team.
On domestic worker training, Bangladesh promised to shorten the training period while improving its quality.
Asif Nazrul reiterated Bangladesh's interest in more skilled workers being recruited for Saudi mega projects.

The adviser asked the Saudi Interior Ministry for help in quick repatriation of irregular migrants; the vice minister promised to review it. He also requested a royal pardon for Bangladeshi prisoners convicted of minor offences in Saudi Arabia, which the vice minister said he would consider.

Bangladesh proposed stronger monitoring to prevent labour exploitation and ensure fair recruitment. Both sides agreed to work together against human trafficking, irregular migration and money laundering, building on the security cooperation agreement signed in November 2022.
Asif Nazrul met Oman's Deputy Minister of Labour Salim Al-Busaidi and asked that irregular Bangladeshi workers be regularised without fines; the Omani minister responded positively.

Work visas for Bangladeshis in Oman have been temporarily suspended since 31 October 2023. Asif Nazrul asked Oman to reopen them; the Omani deputy labour minister said there is pressure from his country's people because of the large demand for Bangladeshi workers and they are looking for a solution.

The adviser asked Oman's cooperation so that skilled Bangladeshis such as engineers, doctors and nurses can enter Oman's labour market; both sides agreed to take steps on information exchange and cooperation.

headline_en: Overseas employment fell, remittances rose; only the Saudi labour market is open
summary_en: BMET data show overseas employment fell by about three lakh in 2024 to about 10 lakh after Malaysia, UAE and Oman closed, leaving Saudi Arabia as the only large open market. Remittances nevertheless hit a record USD 26.7 billion in 2024. BAIRA and RMMRU warn against dependence on a single market.

facts.statement: BMET data: 6 lakh 17 thousand workers went abroad in 2021, more than 11 lakh in 2022, more than 13 lakh in 2023, and about 10 lakh in 2024 (three lakh fewer than 2023).
In 2024, 90 percent of Bangladeshi workers who went abroad went to just five countries: Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Qatar, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates.
As of early January 2025 the labour markets of Malaysia and the UAE are closed to Bangladeshi workers and recruitment to Oman is also closed; among large markets only Saudi Arabia is open.
More than 3.5 lakh workers went to Malaysia in 2023; the market has been closed since June 2024 and fewer than one lakh went in all of 2024, a drop of more than two lakh.
More than 1.25 lakh workers went to Oman in 2023; with the market closed, only 358 went in 2024.
About one lakh Bangladeshi workers went to the UAE in 2023; 47 thousand went in 2024.
About 5 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Saudi Arabia in 2023 and more than 6.25 lakh in 2024. In the last three months of 2024, more than 80 percent of all overseas employment was in Saudi Arabia.

There are complaints that workers in Saudi Arabia do not get work as per contract, become illegal, are detained by Saudi police and are sent home. Saudi Arabia tops the list of countries from which workers return empty-handed without a passport.

Saudi Arabia is host of the 2034 football World Cup and preparation of football infrastructure has begun, bringing regular demand for workers; people concerned think sending workers to Saudi Arabia may fall after June 2025.

Although the government claims workers are sent to 168 countries, in 2024 workers went to 135 countries: one worker each to 14 countries, two each to another 14, at least 10 thousand to only 8 countries, and more than one lakh only to Saudi Arabia.
BAIRA Secretary General Ali Haider Chowdhury said nearly all labour markets except Saudi Arabia are closed, that a Saudi closure would cause a disaster, and that alternative markets must be built.

Remittances in 2024 totalled USD 2,670 crore (26.7 billion), the highest ever; the previous peak was just over USD 2,200 crore in 2021. People concerned attribute the rise to less money laundering and less hundi after the political change, so expatriates sent more through formal channels.

RMMRU founding chair Tasneem Siddiqui said dependence on specific labour markets is the biggest weakness, trust in banks has returned and hundi demand has fallen since the political change, and the government should focus on market management.

headline_en: UAE overtakes Saudi Arabia as top remittance source; 'other reasons' suspected
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show the UAE became the top remittance-sending country in FY2023-24, up USD 1.6 billion (about 53%), while Saudi Arabia fell from first to fourth. Bankers and economists doubt the UAE growth reflects workers' earnings, suspecting laundered money returning via Dubai to collect the remittance incentive. BMET worker-outflow figures for UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Malaysia and the UK are given.

facts.statement: In FY2023-24 the UAE was the top source of remittances to Bangladesh, up from third in FY2022-23; remittances from the UAE rose by USD 160 crore or about 53 percent in a year.
In FY2023-24 the United States was the second largest remittance source at about USD 296 crore and the United Kingdom third at USD 279 crore.
Saudi Arabia, the top remittance source in FY2022-23, fell to fourth in FY2023-24; remittances through legal channels from Saudi Arabia fell by USD 103 crore or about 27 percent in a year.

BMET data: just over 1 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to the UAE in 2022, 98 thousand in 2023, and about 33.5 thousand in January-June 2024. From 2004 to June 2024 about 21.5 lakh went to the UAE, against about 39 lakh to Saudi Arabia in the same period.

Mutual Trust Bank managing director Syed Mahbubur Rahman said the growth in UAE remittances does not look like only workers' money. Economists and labour market experts say Dubai has become a new destination for money laundered from Bangladesh, and part of it may be returning through legal channels to take the remittance incentive and then leaving again illegally.

CPD research director Khondaker Golam Moazzem said the government gives an incentive on remittances and banks give a separate incentive on top, and the central bank is somewhat lenient; Bangladesh Bank could investigate whether laundered money from Dubai is coming in as remittance.

Among the top 10 remittance source countries in FY2023-24, remittances fell from Saudi Arabia, the United States, Qatar and Kuwait and rose from the other six. Oman had the second highest growth; Malaysia grew 35 percent and the UK 34 percent.
BMET data: more than 3 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Oman in 2022 and 2023 combined, the most since 2016.
More than 3.5 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia in 2023, the highest in the 20 years 2004-2023.
More than 10 thousand Bangladeshi workers went to the United Kingdom in 2023, the highest in 20 years.

headline_en: I don't know any MPs; action will be taken if responsible: Expatriates' Welfare State Minister
summary_en: At a 2 June 2024 press conference on the Malaysia labour market, State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said those responsible for irregularities would face action and announced a six-member inquiry committee. The ministry gave figures: 101 agencies got approval for 526,676 workers, 493,642 got BMET clearance, 476,672 went and 16,970 could not go within the deadline. The secretary said agencies will refund those who had clearance but could not go.

facts.statement: After the Malaysia market reopened this time, 101 agencies took approval for 526,676 workers; Malaysia did not give final approval for all, so BMET clearance was taken for 493,642 workers, of whom 476,672 went to Malaysia and 16,970 could not go within the set deadline.

The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry formed a 6-member inquiry committee on Sunday 2 June 2024, headed by Additional Secretary (Employment) Nur Md. Mahbubul Haque, to find corruption and irregularities in the Malaysia labour market; it must report within 7 working days, will work to ensure compensation for affected workers, and will recommend what to do in such situations in future.
The government-set cost for going to Malaysia is BDT 78,990; a worker charged more than this can report it to the ministry's inquiry committee, and anyone can lodge a complaint with the committee.

Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin said recruiting agencies will refund the money of those who got clearance but could not go to Malaysia; BAIRA has taken responsibility for this, and legal action will be taken if the money is not refunded.

The secretary said no permission was given to send workers in the name of companies blacklisted by Malaysia. A recruiting agency must get approval from the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry before sending workers to Malaysia.

On workers not getting jobs in Malaysia, the secretary said employers come to the airport there to receive workers and in the past few months there was no case of a worker not being received; work is being arranged for the five thousand workers who earlier did not get jobs.

State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said clearance was given whenever sought; 23 special flights were arranged after talks with the civil aviation ministry and Biman Bangladesh, and a letter was sent a week earlier asking Malaysia to extend the deadline by one week.

There are allegations of a syndicate in sending workers to Malaysia with widespread irregularities and business worth thousands of crores of taka, with four Members of Parliament involved (not named in this article). The state minister said 'I do not believe in syndicates; if the receiving country wants to take workers through agencies of its choice, that is its matter', and did not give a specific answer on whether a syndicate would form again.
The state minister said the Malaysia labour market will open and the government is working on it.

headline_en: What stops Bangladeshi workers from going to South Korea
summary_en: A column by North South University migration researchers on South Korea's Employment Permit System (EPS), under which BOESL alone sends Bangladeshi workers. It gives numbers sent, Korean labour shortages by sector, remittance figures, the obstacles (quota depends on diplomacy, employer preference for Vietnam or Nepal, weak practical Korean), and recommendations.

facts.statement: According to BMET's 2023 report, on average eight lakh Bangladeshis a year went abroad for long and short term employment from 2014 to 2023; about 80 percent work in Gulf and Middle East countries.
Only 53,678 Bangladeshis went to South Korea as migrant workers from 1994 to 2023, mainly through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) under the Employment Permit System (EPS).
Bangladesh is unable to fill the quota allocated to it under South Korea's EPS.

The Employment Permit System (EPS) is South Korea's legal arrangement for recruiting foreign workers, based on bilateral labour agreements with 16 countries including Bangladesh, China, Nepal and Pakistan; each country gets a yearly quota. The quota is decided by the Korean government according to sector needs.
Since the first Bangladesh-South Korea bilateral agreement in 2007, BOESL has been the sole sender of workers to South Korea's industry, construction and agriculture sectors.
From 2015 to 2022 a total of 105,891 migrant workers from Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka went to South Korea under EPS; Bangladesh sent far fewer than Nepal.
Under EPS, 1,647 Bangladeshis went to Korea in 2019, 208 in 2020, 108 in 2021 and 5,910 in 2022.

According to the South Korean labour ministry's June 2022 data, shortages were 4,800 workers in shipbuilding, 27,000 in manufacturing, 14,200 in food and small cottage industry and about 2,300 in transport; the Korean government eased administrative rules for hiring foreign workers.
facts.source_in_article: South Korean labour ministry, cited by authors

facts.statement: In 2022 the Korean government arranged E-9 visas for 69 thousand foreign workers, more than the previous year's quota. In 2023 it increased the quota for Bangladeshi workers by 10 thousand.
Migrants returned from South Korea say that working there for more than four years makes it possible to earn at least BDT one crore.
facts.source_in_article: Returned migrants interviewed by the authors

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank data: remittances from South Korea were USD 96.29 million in FY2017-18 and USD 135.46 million in FY2021-22.

Studies show some Korean employers believe Bangladeshi workers do not properly follow Korean cultural and work norms, so Bangladeshis may not be the first choice and employers often prefer workers from Vietnam or Nepal.

Under EPS, the first and main qualification for a job in Korea is Korean language ability; candidates must pass a Korean language test. Many who pass still lack practical language skill, and regional dialects and pronunciation in Korean cities make it hard to understand.

The authors recommend diplomatic efforts to raise the quota, better Korean language training (more TTCs, teachers and equipment, private sector courses, BOESL monitoring of language courses), priority for technically trained candidates, research on Korean labour demand, Korean investment in language and training centres, and using long-settled Bangladeshis in Korea to brand Bangladesh.
The authors say Bangladesh's migrant labour market has become mainly Middle East-based, where workers' earnings are steadily falling.

headline_en: Foreign minister calls for easier visa process for Bangladeshi workers in the UAE
summary_en: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud met UAE human resources minister Abdulrahman Al Awar in Dubai on Friday 8 March 2024 and asked for visas to be reopened for Bangladeshi workers of all categories in all trades, an easier visa process and easier transfer of work permits between employers. The UAE minister said there is no bar on employing Bangladeshis and that the UAE is emphasising skilled recruitment.

facts.statement: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud asked UAE Minister of Human Resources Abdulrahman Al Awar, at a meeting in the minister's office in Dubai on Friday morning 8 March 2024, to reopen visas for Bangladeshi workers of all categories in all trades in the UAE, simplify the visa process, and ease transfer of work permits from one employer to another.

The UAE human resources minister said there is no bar on employment of Bangladeshi workers and that the UAE government is emphasising recruitment of skilled workers based on the demands of a technology-driven job market; he described the use of AI and software in UAE recruitment and management and the method of verifying job seekers' skills.
facts.source_in_article: Abdulrahman Al Awar, via press release

facts.statement: The two ministers discussed recruiting more Bangladeshis in the UAE in all fields, including graduate nurses, caregivers, healthcare technicians, agriculturists and farmers, and various professionals.
Hasan Mahmud told the UAE side about Bangladesh's initiatives to raise the skills of UAE-bound workers and about appointing UAE language trainers to prepare Bangladeshi workers for that job market.

Citing Kuwait's recruitment of Bangladeshi nurses, Hasan Mahmud asked the UAE to recruit qualified nurses and medical professionals from Bangladesh; the UAE minister welcomed the proposal and assured he would examine the Kuwaiti recruitment model at the upcoming joint technical committee meeting in Dhaka.

headline_en: The mistakes that keep Bangladesh from capturing Japan's labour market
summary_en: A column by Dr Selim Reza of North South University arguing that Bangladesh has missed Japan's labour shortage because of weak skills, Japanese language training, costly and opaque recruitment and poor coordination. It recalls the 2005 agreement that sent only 41 workers in eight years, the 2015 IM Japan and 2017 initiatives, and the 27 August 2019 SSW memorandum, and lists four mistakes and recommended fixes.

facts.statement: Under a July 2005 Bangladesh-Japan agreement on technical training and work opportunities for Bangladeshi workers in Japan, only 41 workers were sent in eight years: 12 by the government body BMET and 29 by private recruiting agencies.

In 2015 an understanding was reached with the Japanese organisation IM Japan to train 500 Bangladeshis, and in 2017 a new initiative for one-year training in manufacturing and construction was taken, but Bangladesh could not turn these into large, continuous employment programmes.
A memorandum of cooperation on sending Specified Skilled Workers (SSW) to Japan was signed on 27 August 2019; limits in language teaching, skill testing and transparent recruitment remained.

Surveys of technical trainees from various countries in Japanese immigration authority documents show trainees becoming indebted because of large sums paid to recruiters and intermediaries in their home countries.
facts.source_in_article: Japanese immigration authority documents, cited by author

facts.statement: To work in Japan a candidate must learn Japanese, acquire occupational skills and pass qualifying tests, which takes time; the author says Japanese language is a central condition, needed to understand instructions, stay safe and manage daily life.

The author says Japanese language training opportunities are Dhaka-centred, training is costly and quality teachers are limited; a rural young person often cannot bear the cost of language learning, tests and paperwork, and training quality varies between centres with no guaranteed job afterwards.

The author recommends a five-year measurable action plan for Japan, direct partnerships with Japanese employers and industry bodies, language and skills test access outside Dhaka, financial support for training, full disclosure of recruitment costs, quick action against fraud, contracts that clearly state wage, working hours, housing cost and complaint procedure, and Bangla-language legal aid and grievance handling for workers abroad.

headline_en: Learning the destination's language before working abroad is the key to building a skilled workforce
summary_en: A commentary arguing that most Bangladeshi workers go abroad without training or knowledge of the destination language and so end up in low-paid manual work, while Indian, Filipino and Pakistani workers dominate service jobs in the Middle East. It proposes a compulsory 6-8 month or 1-year language course linked to visa processing, combined with vocational training. It contains no figures, rules in force or cases.

facts.statement: The article says the majority of Bangladeshi workers going abroad go without prior training or knowing the destination country's language, and so are forced into low-wage general manual labour.

The article says that in the Middle East, Indian, Filipino and Pakistani workers dominate service jobs such as transport, supershops, restaurants, construction management, sales and hospitality, mainly because they gain minimum skill in Arabic, English or the destination's main language before going.

The author proposes (not an existing rule) making an intensive language course of 6 to 8 months or 1 year compulsory before going abroad for work, run by government or approved agencies, and linking a language certificate to visa processing.

The author states that a worker with language skill and technical knowledge can earn two or three times what an unskilled general worker earns; suggested trades are plumbing, electrical wiring, welding, air-conditioning repair, mechanic, caregiving, driving and computer operating.

The author says workers who do not know the language sometimes suffer serious accidents because they cannot understand factory safety instructions, and many get into legal trouble from not understanding local law and culture; knowing the language lets a worker speak up for rights and reach the authorities.

headline_en: They hold people hostage in Libya and take ransom at home, building houses, cars and farms
summary_en: A Prothom Alo investigation into a trafficking ring led by Alauddin Sheikh and Awal Faraji of Kalia, Narail, which lured people with Italy, held them hostage in Libya, sent torture videos to families and collected ransom. CID filed a case against 34 people on 13 April 2026 and found more than BDT 376.5 crore moved through at least 114 bank accounts in five years across 11 districts, mixed with hundi. A BRAC study of 557 Libya returnees and one family's BDT 75 lakh ransom are reported.

facts.statement: Prothom Alo's investigation found that Alauddin Sheikh and his ring took people to Libya on the promise of sending them to Italy, held them hostage, sent videos of them being tortured to family members and collected lakhs of taka in ransom; ring members built houses, bought cars and set up farms with the money.

On 13 April 2026 the police Criminal Investigation Department (CID) filed a case against 34 people including Alauddin Sheikh and Awal Faraji. CID found the ring transacted more than BDT 376 crore 50 lakh through various bank accounts in the last five years, with members spread across 11 districts.
Organisations working on migrant workers' rights estimate that more than fifty such hostage-and-ransom rings are active in different parts of Bangladesh.

CID Financial Crime division Additional DIG Muhammad Basir Uddin said a case has been filed against a trafficking ring involved in ransom-taking in Libya and hundi, and an inquiry into the members' assets is under way.

Alauddin Sheikh of Satbaria, Kalia upazila, Narail has a walled two-storey house with CCTV at Satbaria bazar, a cattle farm beside it, a second farm under construction on about one bigha, a luxury house in Khulna and an expensive car; his father Ali Sheikh said the family lived on farming before the son went abroad. CID says Alauddin went to Libya 12 years ago, later joined Awal in trafficking, heads the ring, and handled holding victims in Libya, collecting ransom and coordinating with members at home.

Alauddin Sheikh told Prothom Alo on 30 July 2026 that he had a big job in Libya with a high salary and built his house and farm from that. His father Ali Sheikh claimed Alauddin was a contractor in Libya and that workers' money came to his (Ali Sheikh's) bank account for their families, which got called hundi; he said he once faced a case and stopped this five or six years ago.

Awal Faraji of Satbaria village, Kalia, Narail, built a two-storey house; his brothers Rabbani Faraji and Rubel Faraji are involved in the ring. His mother Haricha Begum said he used to take people abroad and gave it up after returning home about a year ago, and that her son Rabbani was arrested over 'account business'. Awal has been in hiding since his brother's arrest.

CID found the ransom money moved through at least 114 bank accounts, including accounts of ring members, their businesses, housewives, grocers and a pharmacy owner, many of them relatives or acquaintances; the ring paid a commission of BDT 500 to 1,000 per lakh to use these accounts, deliberately using many people's accounts to hide the source.
An investigating officer said the bank account of a shop called Shukur Medical Hall in Narail saw about BDT two crore in transactions in the last two years.

CID says trafficking, hostage ransom and hundi were run through the same network: ring members went village to village luring people, took lakhs of taka and sent them to Awal and Alauddin in Libya, then collected ransom from families. CID identified 18 businesses, which exist in name only with trade licences, used for ransom and hundi transactions; they and their owners are accused in the case.

Amena Begum of Muksudpur, Gopalganj contracted with brokers to send five family members (including two grandsons) to Italy at BDT 18 lakh each, BDT 90 lakh in total, and paid by selling land and borrowing. They were taken to Libya and held hostage, and torture videos were sent demanding more money. She said on 15 July 2026 that she sent BDT 75 lakh to the bank accounts of ring members Mina Begum, Nurul Islam and Murad Mia, after which her family members were sent across the Mediterranean to Italy by boat. (The section heading calls the BDT 75 lakh ransom; the text gives both the BDT 90 lakh contract and the BDT 75 lakh sent.)

A BRAC study of 557 Bangladeshis returned from Libya found: families of 60 percent had been promised good jobs by local brokers; 89 percent got no job or work on reaching Libya; 63 percent were taken captive on the way; of the captives 93 percent were held in camps and 79 percent were physically tortured; 68 percent lost freedom of movement after arrival; 54 percent never got three meals a day and 22 percent got only one meal a day.

Shariful Islam, associate director of BRAC Migration Programme and Youth Platform, said there are more than a hundred camps in Libya where people are held hostage and tortured, and ransoms of BDT 5 lakh to 76 lakh have been taken from families; he said those involved must be brought to justice and their assets confiscated.

headline_en: What happens to us if Middle East countries cut back on taking workers
summary_en: A column by Selim Reza of North South University warning that Gulf demand for low-skilled foreign workers is shrinking because of nationalisation policies (Saudisation and equivalents), automation and AI, maturing construction projects and the US-Iran war. It cites ILO figures and describes how the Philippines, India, Vietnam, Nepal and Pakistan prepare skilled workers, and lists five recommendations.

facts.statement: According to government data, close to 10 lakh Bangladeshis a year have gone abroad for work in recent years, mostly to Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain and other Gulf countries, from which more than half of total remittances come; most are low-skilled or semi-skilled.
facts.source_in_article: Government data, cited by author Selim Reza

facts.statement: Gulf countries are running nationalisation policies that prioritise jobs for their own citizens: Saudisation in Saudi Arabia, Qatarisation in Qatar, Emiratisation in the UAE, Kuwaitisation in Kuwait and Omanisation in Oman, aiming by 2030 to raise citizens' employment in public and private sectors and cut dependence on foreign workers. Saudi Arabia is also moving under Vision 2030 toward technology, tourism, digital services and advanced industry.

The author says demand for large numbers of construction workers in the Middle East is no longer what it was because big infrastructure projects are reaching a mature stage, and automation, smart logistics and AI are reducing repetitive low-skilled jobs.

An ILO 2025 study found that within a year or two about 14.6 percent of jobs in the Arab region (about 80 lakh) will become more technology-dependent through AI, and about 2.2 percent (about 12 lakh) are at risk of being eliminated or replaced by automation.

A recent ILO report estimates about 40 percent of employment in the Arab region is concentrated in high-risk sectors such as construction, manufacturing, transport, trade and hospitality, where foreign workers are most present.

ILO's 2026 forecast: if the US-Iran war is prolonged, total working hours in the Arab region could fall by up to 3.7 percent, and in a worse scenario by 10.2 percent, larger than the Covid-19 shock. ILO warned migrant workers will bear the biggest burden, with early signs of reduced new hiring and weaker remittance flows.

The author says demand is rising across the Arab world for industrial automation technicians, advanced welders, electrical and mechanical technicians, healthcare workers, renewable energy specialists, logistics operators, IT-skilled workers and digital maintenance specialists.

The author describes competitors: the Philippines trains nurses, caregivers, marine engineers, IT specialists and technical workers to specific country demand; Nepal runs a joint programme with ILO on safe migration, skills certification, social protection and fair recruitment for the Gulf; Pakistan is implementing a roadmap for AI-based job matching, digital certificate verification, online pre-departure training and a digital recruitment platform, and stresses mutual recognition of skills with Gulf countries.

The author recommends demand-based skills development ('skills diplomacy'), internationally recognised technical certification, making language (English, Arabic), digital skills, workplace safety and soft skills a compulsory part of migration preparation, joint training with foreign industries and institutions, and treating migration as a coordinated strategy across ministries.

summary_en: Answering questions in parliament on Wednesday 15 April 2026, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said that given unrest in Iran and the Middle East the government has plans for alternative labour markets: bilateral agreements with countries such as Serbia, Greece, North Macedonia, Romania, Portugal, Brazil and Russia, an agreement with Thailand, work to reopen Malaysia, and expanded Japanese language and skills training. The rest of the article covers unrelated parliamentary answers (teachers, blue economy, e-health card, playgrounds, PayPal).

The Prime Minister said the government is working to reopen the Malaysia labour market; the minister and adviser in charge of the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry visited Malaysia on 8-11 April 2026, which he said will ease the way to send Bangladeshi workers through bilateral talks.
The Prime Minister said that because of large demand for Bangladeshi workers in Japan, the scope of Japanese language and skills training has been expanded to raise the rate of sending workers there.

The Prime Minister said Bangladesh embassies have been instructed to survey labour markets and assess occupation-wise demand for Bangladeshi workers, and there is a plan to appoint country-based local lobbyists or specialist firms as needed on the recommendation of Bangladesh missions abroad.
The Prime Minister said a committee has been formed to take effective steps to start PayPal's operations in Bangladesh (and to run hi-tech/software parks and ICT centres).

headline_en: Took BDT 50 lakh promising Italy, then held and tortured in a detention house; young man dies
summary_en: Md. Zahirul Akon (28) of Dasar upazila, Madaripur died on Sunday 5 April 2026 in a detention house in Libya after torture for ransom, on an irregular route to Italy via Saudi Arabia. His family paid local broker Zakir Matubbar BDT 25 lakh under the contract and another BDT 25 lakh as ransom. The brokers, who work for Habibur Rahman Khandaker alias Habib Master, are in hiding; police say they will arrest them once the family complains.

facts.statement: Md. Zahirul Akon (28), youngest son of Shamsul Haque Akon of Dakshin Dhuasa village, Baligram union, Dasar upazila, Madaripur, died on Sunday (5 April 2026) in a detention house in Libya under brokers' torture while on an illegal route to Italy; the family got the news on Monday night 6 April 2026.
In the month before Zahirul Akon's death, two other young men from Dasar and Kalkini upazilas of Madaripur died in Libya under brokers' torture for ransom money.

Local brokers Tarak Das and Zakir Matubbar of Baligram, Dasar upazila lured Zahirul Akon about six months before April 2026 with a promise to get him to Italy in just 17 days 'without any trouble' under a BDT 25 lakh contract.
facts.source_in_article: Brother Jalal Akon; family and local sources

facts.statement: The broker ring first took Zahirul Akon from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia, kept him there a few days, then flew him from Saudi Arabia to Libya. He was then kept about three and a half months in a detention house on the promise of a boat crossing from the Libyan coast to Italy, without being tortured. About one and a half months before his death, on the way to the Libyan coast, he was taken hostage by local 'mafia' and held in a secret detention house and tortured for ransom. (His brother describes the captors as Bangladeshi 'mafia' brokers living in Libya.)

Zahirul Akon's family paid BDT 25 lakh under the contract up front; the captors then sent a torture video and demanded BDT 25 lakh ransom, which the family paid through local broker Zakir Matubbar in two instalments, BDT 15 lakh then BDT 10 lakh. In total BDT 50 lakh was paid, and he was still not freed.

Broker Zakir Matubbar himself told the family of Zahirul's death and proposed a settlement; when the family refused and the matter became known, Zakir Matubbar and Tarak Das went into hiding. Both have long been involved in a trafficking ring and work for another local broker, Habibur Rahman Khandaker alias Habib Master of Gopalpur, Dasar upazila.

Habibur Rahman Khandaker alias Habib Master, a former madrasa teacher of Gopalpur, Dasar upazila, Madaripur, is described as a key Bangladesh-based member of the Libya trafficking ring, long active and beyond police reach. Local residents say he has sent at least three hundred young men from Kalkini and Dasar upazilas to Italy via Libya and at least a hundred of his migrants are still in detention houses in Libya. The phones of all three brokers were switched off.

Madaripur Additional SP (Crime and Ops) Jahangir Alam said police learned of the death from relatives, will give any legal help the family asks for, have a zero-tolerance policy on brokers and will arrest them as soon as a complaint is received from the family. No case had been filed at the time of the report.
Zahirul Akon's relatives have asked for the government's help to bring his body home and for the maximum punishment of the broker.

Zahirul Akon had a BA from a local college, had served in Ansar, left the job and farmed with his elder brother; he leaves a wife, Sathi Akter, and two daughters (the article gives their ages as 10 months for the elder and six years for the younger, as printed).

summary_en: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Md. Nurul Haque Nur said on 24 March 2026 that the Prime Minister has directed loans of up to BDT 10 lakh through Probashi Kallyan Bank for students going abroad, as proof of bank solvency, paid toward tuition and other payments rather than in cash. headline_en: Online services for going abroad for work will be free of charge
summary_en: The Overseas Employment Platform (OEP), built under the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry with ILO Bangladesh and the Swiss government, was formally launched in Dhaka on 19 November 2025; it has been running since 19 April 2025. Workers register free with a mobile number, pay BDT 200 online for BMET registration, apply for BMET clearance and download the smart card. It replaces the 'Ami Probashi' app, which charged a private company's fee. Asif Nazrul also said Bangladesh has objected to some of Malaysia's 10 conditions.

facts.statement: The Overseas Employment Platform (OEP), a national integrated digital gateway covering the whole process of going abroad for work, was formally inaugurated on Wednesday 19 November 2025 at a hotel in Dhaka. It was built under the leadership of the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry as a joint initiative of ILO Bangladesh and the government of Switzerland. Workers get the online service free of charge.

On OEP, a worker first registers with their own mobile number, which opens a profile where personal information is added; then takes BMET registration online by paying a BDT 200 fee; then can apply for BMET clearance and download the clearance smart card from the platform.
BMET registration through the OEP platform costs BDT 200, paid online; use of the platform itself is free.

Foreign employers can register on OEP; after the embassy attests them they can submit a demand letter, which goes to recruiting agencies. Workers can contact recruiting agencies directly for jobs through the platform and can enrol in a TTC through it.

OEP connects aspiring migrant workers, recruiting agencies, BMET, Technical Training Centres (TTC), foreign employers, immigration authorities and return or reintegration service providers. All its data will be held by BMET.

The 'Ami Probashi' mobile app, through which the previous government offered online BMET clearance and which required a fee to the private company running it on top of the BMET fee, was cancelled by the interim government; the new OEP platform has been in operation since 19 April 2025.

Adviser Asif Nazrul said OEP is completely free, unlike 'Ami Probashi' which charged money and faced allegations of irregularities, and that through OEP a worker can find out that an employer is not fake.

Asif Nazrul said Bangladesh has already objected to several of the 10 conditions Malaysia has set for recruiting agencies and asked for the deadline to be extended, telling Malaysia that if the conditions are followed a syndicate will form again and only a few agencies will get to send workers; Malaysia has promised to relax them.
As shown on the OEP site: 2,647 recruiting agencies have joined; 1,091,161 workers have applied to BMET for clearance and 1,024,468 have received it; 837,042 have registered for TTC training.

summary_en: After meetings with three Malaysian ministers on Thursday 15 May 2025, Adviser Asif Nazrul said in a Facebook video that Malaysia may take 1 to 1.5 lakh foreign workers in the coming months with top priority for Bangladesh, and that taking 7,926 workers in a first phase (those who earlier could not go) has been finalised. Bangladesh asked that all recruiting agencies be allowed to send workers, for multiple-entry visas and for regularisation of undocumented workers.

facts.statement: Adviser Asif Nazrul said Malaysia may take one to one and a half lakh foreign workers in the next few months and that Malaysian Human Resources Minister Steven Sim Chee Keong assured Bangladesh would get top priority, with the most people taken from Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, Facebook video message after meetings in Malaysia

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said the meeting was told that taking 7,926 workers in the first phase has been finalised and the process has started; these are from the workers who earlier could not go from Bangladesh, whom Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim promised during his Bangladesh visit in 2024 to give a chance to go. Malaysia has said it will take them in phases.
Bangladesh asked Malaysia to allow all recruiting agencies in Bangladesh to send workers; Malaysia said it would consider it well and communicate a decision soon.
Bangladesh proposed that Malaysia take skilled workers including security guards, nurses and caregivers from Bangladesh.

Asif Nazrul said Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia get single-entry visas; he asked the Malaysian home minister to give them multiple-entry visas like workers of other countries, and the home minister immediately instructed his officials to act quickly.

Asked to regularise Bangladeshi workers who have become undocumented, Malaysian ministers said this is done from time to time, most recently in 2024, but cannot be done for those whose visa has expired; Bangladesh asked that these also be considered, as workers often cannot renew visas because of the employer. Malaysia said it would consider it.

A Bangladesh delegation led by Asif Nazrul went to Malaysia on 13 May 2025; on 15 May it held formal meetings with the Malaysian home minister and human resources minister and an informal meeting with the trade minister. Chief Adviser's special envoy on international affairs Lutfey Siddiqi took part.

headline_en: Malaysia labour market may reopen; meeting today
summary_en: A preview of the 15 May 2025 Bangladesh-Malaysia talks in Putrajaya on reopening the Malaysia labour market, closed for over a year. It explains that the existing MoU, valid to December 2025, lets Malaysia choose the agencies, that Bangladesh will propose amending it and letting all valid agencies send workers, and that a joint technical committee is to meet in Dhaka on 21-22 May. It gives past numbers and the gap between the BDT 79,000 official cost and over BDT 5 lakh actually charged.

facts.statement: The Malaysia labour market has been closed for more than a year; a three-member Bangladesh delegation led by Adviser Asif Nazrul (with Senior Secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan and Deputy Secretary Md. Sarwar Alam) went to Malaysia on Tuesday 13 May 2025 and was due to meet the Malaysian human resources minister and home minister in Putrajaya on 15 May. Ministry officials hope sending workers can start under the existing MoU after the meeting.

Malaysia used to take workers from 14 countries; the article says Malaysian authorities closed the labour market for all including Bangladesh 'at the start of 2024', when allegations of a syndicate in sending workers had arisen. (The same article says workers went until May 2024.)

The MoU signed between Bangladesh and Malaysia on sending workers gives the Malaysian government the responsibility for selecting agencies; it is valid until December 2025, so there is no scope for a new agreement, but Bangladesh will propose some amendment and will propose at the joint technical committee that all valid agencies be allowed to send workers.

Malaysia proposed holding the joint technical committee meeting in Dhaka on 21-22 May 2025 and Bangladesh agreed, according to a ministry letter to the Bangladesh High Commissioner in Malaysia; the committee will discuss the process of sending workers. Bangladesh had written to Malaysia several times before Malaysia agreed in April 2025.

About 13 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia from 2004 to May 2024; the highest in one year was more than 3.5 lakh in 2023. Before the first closure, more than four lakh went in 2007 and 2008; before the second, about three lakh in 2017 and 2018; and about five lakh went between August 2022 and May 2024.
When the Malaysia market last opened in 2022 the government set the cost of sending a worker to Malaysia at BDT 79 thousand.
Various studies later found that agencies took on average more than BDT five lakh from each worker going to Malaysia, against the official BDT 79 thousand.

Recruiting agency owners think several lakh more workers can be sent to Malaysia and say the main challenge is reducing migration cost. 23 non-government organisations working with migrants made 10 recommendations to the government on reopening the Malaysia market. RMMRU acting executive director Tasneem Siddiqui said the opportunity must not be limited to certain firms as before and workers' cost must be kept limited.

headline_en: 23 bodies recovered in Libya: BDT 16 lakh 'body contract' from Dhaka to Italy
summary_en: Explains the 'body contract' used by brokers on the Libya-Italy route through the cases of Kuddus Bepari (missing) and his brother-in-law Sujon Howlader (dead) of Rajoir, Madaripur, who each contracted with broker Monir Sheikh for BDT 16 lakh and were on the boat that sank after leaving Benghazi on 24 January 2025. It profiles Monir Sheikh, his three Libya-based sons-in-law and other ring members, quotes an unnamed broker on the 12 lakh plus 4 lakh price split, and reports that no family had yet filed a case.

facts.statement: Brokers on the Libya-Mediterranean route use a 'body contract': the broker takes a fixed sum on the promise of delivering the migrant alive to Italy however long it takes, and until then the broker ring bears the migrant's lodging, food and air fare. The route mainly uses small boats loaded beyond capacity.
Broker Monir Sheikh of Rajoir, Madaripur makes each 'body contract' for Dhaka to Italy via Libya at BDT 16 lakh.

A local broker of another Italy-sending ring, speaking anonymously, said they take BDT 12 lakh in the first stage to send a person as far as Libya and then BDT 4 lakh for the 'game' (the sea crossing of the Mediterranean); local brokers collect people and money and work through Bangladeshi brokers living in Libya, while the 'mafia' in Libya do the main work.

Kuddus Bepari was sent from Dhaka first to Egypt in early November 2024; his brother-in-law Sujon Howlader left home on 20 December 2024 and was also taken from Dhaka via Egypt to Libya. After about two months in a detention house ('game ghor') they were taken to the Benghazi coast on 24 January 2025 and put on an engine boat, which sank in the Mediterranean a few hours later; 23 bodies have washed up on the Libyan coast so far.

To pay broker Monir, Kuddus Bepari (33) signed over his two bighas of land, valued at BDT 40 lakh, to Monir's wife Hamida Begum; his contract was BDT 16 lakh. Sujon Howlader (39) paid Monir BDT 16 lakh, borrowed, under a body contract.

Sujon Howlader (39) died in the boat sinking, confirmed by his wife Munni Begum; Kuddus Bepari (33) has been missing since and his family believes he is dead, as people who were in the detention house with him said he is no more.

Monir Sheikh, son of Haidar Sheikh of Majumdarkandi, Rajoir, ran a tailoring shop at Rajoir bazar until two years ago; after marrying his three daughters to men living in Libya he became a trafficking broker. Locals say his three sons-in-law are linked with traffickers and 'mafia' in Libya; Monir lures people locally and sends them via the sons-in-law. In the last 7 months he bought land worth at least BDT 5 crore in Rajoir municipality and Tekerhat port in his wife Hamida Begum's name. He has been in hiding with his family since the 23 bodies washed ashore, and a neighbour says he is approaching people to settle the matter.
Locals say others in Monir Sheikh's ring include Swapan Matubbar of Haridasdi, Rajoir; Rafiqul Islam of Alipur, Bhanga upazila, Faridpur; and Ambia Begum of Pearpur, Madaripur Sadar.

An unnamed local broker said Miraj Howlader, son of Hossain Howlader of Mridhakandi village, Shikarmangal union, Kalkini upazila, is a big 'mafia' in Libya who has long done this work, and most local brokers in Madaripur now work for him.

Madaripur Additional SP (Administration and Finance) Bhaskar Saha said cases are being accepted for trafficking incidents but no one had yet come to file a case over the recent deaths and disappearances; from families, police know of three dead and seven missing in Rajoir upazila and think the missing are also dead. Police have the names of several brokers and operations to catch them continue.

Kuddus Bepari had worked in Malaysia for 7 years and came home in August 2024 to see his newborn; he was frustrated because the labour market situation in Malaysia was not going well, which the broker exploited.

headline_en: Huge scope to send skilled and semi-skilled workers to Saudi Arabia: Asif Nazrul
summary_en: Per a foreign ministry release of 29 January 2025, Adviser Asif Nazrul told owners and top officials of Saudi companies at a Bangladesh embassy event in Riyadh that there is wide scope to send doctors, engineers, nurses, technicians and other skilled and semi-skilled workers. He inaugurated the embassy's e-demand attestation system and heard expatriates' complaints about high air fares and overcharging by recruiting agencies.

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul inaugurated the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh's e-Demand Attestation System, through which Saudi companies can register online and get worker demand letters attested without going to the embassy.

Asif Nazrul said there is wide scope to send skilled and semi-skilled workers including doctors, engineers, nurses and technicians to Saudi Arabia, pointing to Vision 2030 mega projects, the Roshn project, the 2027 AFC Asian Cup, the 2029 Asian Winter Games, World Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, via foreign ministry release

facts.statement: Saudi recruiting companies acknowledged the presence of skilled Bangladeshi professionals but cited challenges: lack of information, marketing, lengthy visa processing, language barriers and lack of pre-boarding training. The adviser promised to solve these.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi companies, via foreign ministry release

facts.statement: Bangladeshi expatriates in Saudi Arabia complained to Asif Nazrul about high air ticket prices and recruiting agencies charging extra money; he promised solutions.
Asif Nazrul urged expatriates in Saudi Arabia to use social media and the website to increase contact with the embassy, to obey Saudi law and culture and not to get involved in any unlawful activity.

On expatriates' voting rights in national elections, Asif Nazrul said the government is examining possible options to reach a realistic decision. He was in Saudi Arabia at the invitation of the Saudi human resources and social development minister to attend the Global Labour Market Conference.

headline_en: 8 Bangladeshis die in boat sinking off the Libyan coast
summary_en: The foreign ministry spokesperson said on 24 December 2024 that a boat carrying 121 migrants wrecked in the Mediterranean off Libya on 18 December 2024; 82 were rescued alive and at least 15 bodies recovered. A Red Crescent volunteer confirmed to the embassy that 8 of the dead and 32 of the rescued are Bangladeshi.

facts.statement: A boat carrying 121 migrants wrecked in the Mediterranean off the Libyan coast on 18 December 2024. The Libyan navy rescued 82 alive and recovered at least 15 bodies. A local Red Crescent Society volunteer confirmed to the Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli that 8 of the dead are Bangladeshi and 32 of the rescued are Bangladeshi.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign ministry spokesperson Mohammad Rafiqul Alam, weekly briefing 24 Dec 2024

facts.statement: The survivors are being kept in Zawiya city (Jawaiya, as printed), 80 km west of Tripoli, and the bodies at Zawiya hospital; more Bangladeshis are feared to be among the missing.

The Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli is working to confirm the identities of the dead Bangladeshis, and embassy officials are trying to meet the survivors after getting permission from Libya's foreign ministry.

headline_en: 37 young men taken to Libya on the promise of Italy and held hostage; relatives in a dilemma
summary_en: Families of 37 men from three villages of Alamdanga upazila, Chuadanga, told a press conference on Thursday 12 December 2024 that brokers took BDT 15 lakh each on the promise of jobs in Italy, took the men to Dubai and then Libya, and have held and tortured them for about nine months, now demanding BDT 22 lakh per family. They name expatriate Md. Sagor as the ringleader and seven relatives as local brokers; an FIR was recorded at Alamdanga police station on 11 December 2024 and the accused are in hiding.

facts.statement: 37 men from Belgachhi, Khejurtala and Char Jadabpur villages of Alamdanga upazila, Chuadanga, including Jewel Rana of Khejurtala (Nagdah union), are being held hostage by a ring in Libya; Jewel has been held and tortured for 9 months, with large ransoms taken in instalments.
facts.source_in_article: Victims' families at a press conference at Chuadanga Press Club

facts.statement: The brokers lured the men with jobs in Italy paying BDT one to one and a half lakh a month and took BDT 15 lakh from each; instead of Italy they were taken first to Dubai and then to Libya and held hostage, with physical and mental torture.

While hostage, BDT four to five thousand per person per week is extracted for food. For release, BDT 22 lakh per family has been demanded; for the money the men are tortured on video call, including showing finger and toe nails being pulled out.

Relatives allege that expatriate Md. Sagor, son of Md. Jantu of Belgachhi village, Alamdanga, is the ringleader; Jantu, his wife Amena Khatun, son Jibon Ahmed, brother Md. Thantu, Thantu's wife Bedana Khatun (assistant teacher at Belgachhi Government Primary School) and son Jim are local brokers. These seven (as the article counts them) took the money from the families on Sagor's behalf.

Rezaul Haque, father of victim Tuhin, filed a written complaint at Alamdanga police station naming the seven and some unidentified persons; it was recorded as an FIR on Wednesday 11 December 2024. OC Masudur Rahman said the human trafficking case has been taken up, the accused's houses were raided with family members present, and the accused have gone into hiding since the case.
facts.source_in_article: Alamdanga police station OC Masudur Rahman; reporter

facts.statement: Kalpana Khatun of Khejurtala said her son, who got GPA-5 in SSC and had enrolled in college, left for Italy at the end of February 2024 lured by broker Sagor; she sold 10 kathas of land and borrowed from two NGOs to send him, and at least BDT one lakh more was taken for food costs over 9 months. She is now fleeing creditors.

Sabina Khatun of Char Jadabpur said she mortgaged land, sold cattle and borrowed to pay BDT 15 lakh to send her brother. Abdul Majid of Khejurtala said the broker told him his son-in-law would earn BDT one and a half lakh a month right after arriving, so he borrowed from 'Agun-Pani Samiti' at a high interest of BDT 15 thousand a month per one lakh.

Jewel Rana left for Italy after paying BDT 15 lakh from income and sale of land, after his wife Poli Khatun contacted the broker; the ring now claims he will be freed if a further BDT 22 lakh is paid.
